unit.title: Attach flexible cables & plugs to electrical machinery appliance and fixtures

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: An 1800 W kettle runs on 110 V. At least what current must its new cord be rated for?
options: About 8 A
About 16.4 A
About 110 A
About 1.8 A

questions.stem: Which cord suits a heavy electric drill that is used on building sites?
options: Thin twin lamp cord with a clear sheath
Telephone cable with solid copper cores
Single-core building wire in a plastic sleeve
Heavy-duty rubber flexible cord

questions.stem: Why is a heat-resistant cord used on an electric iron or a hot plate?

Heat-resistant cord carries more voltage

questions.stem: Why must an appliance cord have flexible cores (many fine strands), not solid building wire?
options: Solid cores carry too little voltage
Flexible cores need no insulation
Solid cores crack when bent again and again
Solid cores cannot be fitted into plugs

questions.stem: A metal-bodied (Class I) appliance needs a new cord. How many cores must the cord have?

Three, including an earth

questions.stem: A double-insulated (Class II) hair dryer needs a new cord. What is correct?

A single-core cord with a metal braid for earth
Any cord at all, as long as it is long enough

questions.stem: Why does a 220 V plug have a different blade pattern from a 110 V plug?

So it can carry more current than a 110 V plug
So it can be fitted without any earth pin
So its cord can be thinner than a 110 V cord

Tape the plug in so it cannot be pulled out

options: It holds a hidden part that must stay sealed
It is not made to be opened and refitted
It is worth more as scrap brass

Old plugs give off harmful fumes in storage
The plug can be sold back to the maker

questions.stem: Why is the earth core left a little longer than the line and neutral cores inside a plug?
options: So it is easier to tell apart from the others
So it reaches the earth pin from any angle
So it can be cut shorter if it is damaged
So it is the last to pull out if dragged

questions.stem: Why should cord ends that go into screw terminals not be tinned with solder?
options: Solder makes the cores too thick to strip
The solder creeps under pressure and loosens
Solder stops the current from flowing

questions.stem: When stripping the outer sheath of a cord, what must you take care to avoid?
options: Leaving the sheath longer than the cores
Stripping the sheath on a clean bench
Nicking the insulation of the cores inside
Using a stripper made for cord sheath

options: None; the insulation reaches the terminal
About 10 mm, so the inspector can see it
Enough to wrap round the screw twice
Any amount, as long as the cover is on

questions.stem: The cord grip in a plug is too big for the thin cord and will not hold it. What should you do?
options: Tighten the grip onto the cores instead
Tie a knot in the cord inside the plug
Wrap tape round the cord to fill the gap
Use the right grip insert or cord

questions.stem: A customer's extension lead has been cut and joined with tape. What should you do?
options: Add more tape so the join is stronger
Leave it, as long as the lead still works
Replace the whole cord with a new one
Solder the join and cover it with paint

questions.stem: A cord connector (a plug and socket pair) is fitted to join two cords. Which way round should it go?
options: Socket half on the supply side
Plug half on the supply side, so it is easy to grip
Either way round, as long as the joint is taped
With two plug halves, so they cannot be mixed up

questions.stem: A detachable cord set for a computer has a cracked sheath. What is the best repair?
options: Tape over the crack and keep using it
Replace it with a set of the same rating
Cut out the crack and join the two ends
Paint the crack with nail varnish

questions.stem: When connecting a new cord inside an appliance, why must the cores be kept away from elements and moving parts?
options: So the appliance is lighter to carry
So the cores can be seen through the vents
Heat and movement can harm the insulation
So the cord can be shorter than the old one

questions.stem: How do you check that the line, neutral and earth cores are on the right pins of a new plug?
options: Look at the colour of the plug's outer case
Plug it in and see whether the appliance works
Shake the plug and listen for loose parts
Test continuity from each pin to its core

questions.stem: The earth continuity from the plug's earth pin to a metal case reads much higher than the cord alone should. What should you check?
options: The earth terminations at both ends
The colour of the line core
The length of the plug's pins
The battery in the appliance

questions.stem: Why do you flex the cord along its length while doing a continuity test?
options: To warm the cord so the reading is steady
To find a broken strand that opens when bent
To straighten the cord before it is labelled
To check the sheath is the right colour

questions.stem: On a Class I appliance with a new cord, the insulation resistance test is usually made between which points?
options: Line and neutral, with earth left open
Earth pin and the appliance's switch
Line and neutral joined, to earth
The two ends of the earth core

questions.stem: Why is a Class II appliance not given an earth continuity test?
options: Its case is too small to clip onto
It is always tested by the maker
Its cord is too short to test
It has no earth connection

questions.stem: Why should the pass label on a tested appliance show the date and who tested it?
options: So users know it was checked and when it is due
So the appliance can be sold later at a higher price
So the maker's warranty is made longer
So the customer knows who to blame if it fails

questions.stem: An extension lead is 30 m long and each core has 0.02 Ω per metre. It feeds a 10 A load. What is the voltage drop in the lead?
options: 6 V

questions.stem: On a 110 V supply, a drop of 12 V along an extension lead is about what percentage?
options: About 1%
About 5%
About 11%
About 22%

questions.stem: Why should a cable reel be fully unwound when it carries close to its full current?
options: Unwinding the reel makes the voltage higher
A coiled cable picks up radio interference
The reel's socket only works when unwound
Coiled cable cannot lose its heat

questions.stem: Which set-up is best for supplying a pressure washer outdoors?
options: Rubber cord, weatherproof parts, GFCI protection
Indoor PVC extension lead laid across the wet yard
Two thin leads joined with tape to reach further
A multi-plug adaptor left out on the wet ground

questions.stem: What cord length is best for a bench grinder fixed near a socket?
options: As long as possible, coiled under the bench
Just long enough to reach without strain
Short enough that the cord is pulled tight
Any length, as long as it is bright orange

questions.stem: Which defect means a cord must be replaced, not just cleaned?
options: Dust and grease on the outer sheath
A small paint mark on the plug's top
Coloured cores showing through the sheath
A cord that has been coiled loosely

questions.stem: During an inspection you find a plug that is warm and browned around one pin. What is the likely cause?
options: The plug has been left out in the sun
The cord is longer than it needs to be
The appliance is used only now and then
A loose connection or worn socket contact

questions.stem: A workshop has 40 portable appliances that must be inspected every 6 months. How many inspections is that each year?
What should an appliance register record for each item?
options: Only its price and the shop it came from
Its ID, place, test dates and results
The name of each person who has used it
Its colour and the length of its cord

questions.stem: A trainee fits a new cord but leaves the cord grip loose. What could happen?
options: The cord will be too short to reach
The appliance will run more slowly
A tug could pull the cores off their terminals
The plug will not fit the socket

questions.stem: How should you check a trainee's rewired plug before it is tested?
options: Plug it in and see whether it sparks
Weigh it to compare with a new plug
Look at the outside of the plug only
Open it and check every part

questions.stem: A machine with a motor capacitor is unplugged for a new cord. What extra step is needed before touching its terminals?
options: Check and discharge the capacitor safely
Run the motor for a minute to warm it up
Wet your hands so the charge runs away
Tap the capacitor with a screwdriver blade

questions.stem: Why should an appliance cord not be run under a carpet or through a closed doorway?
options: It spoils the look of the room
It can be crushed or overheat unseen
It makes the cord harder to unplug
It uses more electricity that way

questions.stem: A new cord switch on a machine has been wired into the neutral by mistake. What is the danger?
options: The machine will run backwards
The switch will wear out in a week
Parts stay live when it is switched off
The machine will draw twice the current

questions.stem: A portable 220 V air compressor needs a new cord and plug. What decides which plug to fit?
options: Whichever plug is cheapest in the store
The colour of the compressor's tank
The plug that came on the old cord, whatever it was
The nameplate, and the outlet's voltage and rating

questions.stem: A pendant light hangs on a flexible cord from a ceiling rose. What must take the fitting's weight?
options: The cord grips, not the terminals
The terminals in the lamp holder
The line core alone
Tape wrapped round the cord

questions.stem: A desk lamp's cord passes through a hole in its metal base. What must be fitted to protect the cord?
options: A layer of paint round the hole
A smooth bush or grommet in the hole
A knot tied in the cord at the hole
Nothing, if the hole has been filed

questions.stem: A customer asks for a longer, thinner cord on a heater so it reaches further. What do you advise?
options: Thinner cord is fine for any heater
Fit the thin cord and add a larger plug
A thin cord may overheat; use a rated one
Use two thin cords joined together

questions.stem: After fitting a new cord, what should the job record show?
options: Only the customer's phone number
The time it took to drive to the job
The colour of the new cord's sheath
Cord, plug and test results

questions.stem: What should be done with old cords removed from appliances?
options: Cut them up, then dispose of them
Keep them in a box to fit to other appliances
Give them to the customer as extension leads
Leave them coiled on the bench for later

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: In a three-core cord for a Class I appliance, which core is connected to the metal case?
A 220 V appliance draws 6 A. What is its power, in watts?
What is the name of the clamp that holds a cord's outer sheath where it enters a plug or appliance?
A 20 m lead has 0.025 Ω per metre in each core and carries 8 A. What is the voltage drop in the lead, in volts?
Which class of appliance is double insulated and has no earth connection?
In workplace appliance testing, what do the letters PAT stand for?
What is the name of the plug-and-socket pair used to join two lengths of flexible cord?
A cord is rated at 10 A. What is the largest load it can supply on 110 V, in watts?
What is the name of the label fixed to an appliance to show it has passed its test?
What is the name of the outer covering that protects the insulated cores of a cord?
A drum holds 50 m of cord. How many 2.5 m cords can be cut from it?
What material is the sheath of a heavy-duty cord for building sites usually made of?
What is the usual name for a removable cord with a plug at one end and a socket that fits into the appliance at the other?
A cord is rated at 13 A. Is it rated high enough for a 2400 W appliance on 220 V? Answer yes or no.
What is the name of the fault where a plug's line and neutral connections have been swapped?

essays.stem: A 2.6 kW, 220 V floor polisher used in a hotel in Montego Bay needs a new cord. Explain how you would choose the cord and plug. Show your figures.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would read the nameplate: 2600 W at 220 V gives 2600 ÷ 220 = about 11.8 A. The cord must be rated for more than this, for example a cord rated at 13 A or above, and the plug and the outlet must suit 220 V at that current. The polisher has a metal body, so it needs a three-core cord with an earth. Because it is dragged across floors, gets wet and is handled a lot, I would choose a heavy-duty rubber-sheathed flexible cord that resists wear, water and cleaning chemicals. The length should be what the user needs to reach the work without extension leads, but not so long that voltage drop or tangling becomes a problem. I would also check the cord fits the appliance's cord grip and entry. The plug must be the 220 V pattern that matches the hotel's outlets, so it cannot go into a 110 V socket.
markingPoints: Works out the current (about 11.8 A) and picks a cord rated above it
Three-core cord with earth for a metal-bodied appliance
Heavy-duty rubber sheath for wear, water and chemicals
Sensible length; fits the cord grip and entry
Plug of the 220 V pattern matching the outlets and rating

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to fit a new cord to a metal-bodied (Class I) appliance, from removing the old cord to the finished job.
essays.modelAnswer: I would unplug the appliance, keep the plug in view, and check for any stored charge. I would note or photograph how the old cord is connected and which terminals it uses, then remove it. I would choose a cord of the same type and rating or better. I would strip the sheath back only as far as needed so the sheath sits inside the cord grip, and strip each core to the length the terminal needs without nicking the strands. I would route the cores away from hot and moving parts, connecting the earth core to the earth terminal with it slightly longer than the others, then line and neutral to their terminals, tightened firmly with no loose strands or bare conductor showing. I would tighten the cord grip on the sheath and refit all covers. At the plug end I would do the same. Finally I would do the dead tests and record them.
markingPoints: Unplugs, keeps plug in view, checks stored charge; records old connections
Chooses a cord of equal or better type and rating
Strips sheath and cores correctly; sheath held in the cord grip
Correct terminals with earth longer; cores routed away from heat and moving parts
Covers refitted; plug fitted correctly; dead tests done and recorded

essays.stem: Describe how you would make up a heavy-duty 110 V extension lead for site use, and how you would test and label it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would choose a three-core heavy-duty rubber-sheathed cord rated for the largest load the lead will supply, and keep the length as short as the job allows to limit voltage drop. I would fit a plug at the supply end and a socket outlet or a weatherproof connector box at the far end, so that no live pins are ever exposed. Both ends need proper cord grips holding the sheath, with the earth core slightly longer, and terminals tight with no loose strands. For outdoor or wet sites, the lead should be used from a GFCI (RCD)-protected outlet or have its own GFCI. I would test the earth continuity from end to end, the continuity of each core while flexing the cord, insulation resistance between the cores joined and earth, and polarity at the socket. Then I would fix a pass label with the date and my name, record it in the register, and coil it loosely.
markingPoints: Heavy-duty rubber cord rated for the load; length kept short
Plug at supply end and socket at far end, so no live pins show
Correct cord grips, earth longer, tight terminals
GFCI (RCD) protection for outdoor or wet use
Tests (earth continuity, core continuity with flexing, insulation, polarity), pass label and register

essays.stem: Explain the inspections and tests you would carry out after fitting a cord and plug, what each shows, and how they differ for Class I and Class II appliances.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with a visual inspection: the cord is the right type and undamaged, the cord grips hold the sheath at both ends, the terminals are tight with no loose strands, and the plug and case are not cracked. For a Class I appliance I would test earth continuity from the plug's earth pin to the metal case with a low-resistance ohmmeter, flexing the cord, to show a fault current has a path back. Then I would test insulation resistance between line and neutral joined and earth, to show there is no leakage to the case. I would check polarity, so the line pin goes to the line terminal and the switch. For a Class II appliance there is no earth, so there is no earth continuity test; the insulation test is made between the joined line and neutral and the outside metal parts, if any, as the maker says. Results are recorded and the function test follows.
markingPoints: Visual inspection points listed
Class I earth continuity test, with flexing, and why
Insulation resistance test between joined line and neutral and earth, and why
Polarity check
Class II: no earth test, insulation test as the maker says; results recorded

essays.stem: Jamaica uses both 110 V and 220 V outlets. Explain the dangers of fitting the wrong plug to an appliance, and how an electrician prevents them.
essays.modelAnswer: If a 110 V appliance is plugged into 220 V, it gets twice its rated voltage and can overheat, burn out or catch fire within seconds. If a 220 V appliance is plugged into 110 V, motors may stall and overheat and heaters will not work properly. If a plug of the wrong current rating is fitted, the cord and plug may overheat. The main protection is that 110 V and 220 V plugs and sockets have different pin patterns, so a plug fits only the right socket. An electrician must always fit the plug that matches the appliance's nameplate voltage and current, and never fit a 110 V plug to a 220 V appliance to make it fit a spare socket, or use adaptors that defeat the pin pattern. Outlets should be labelled where it helps, and customers should be told why the plug matters.
markingPoints: Danger of 110 V appliance on 220 V: overheating, fire
Danger of 220 V appliance on 110 V, and of wrong current rating
Different pin patterns stop wrong connections
Fit the plug matching the nameplate; never defeat the pattern or use unsafe adaptors
Labelling outlets and advising customers

essays.stem: A furniture workshop in Spanish Town asks you to set up an inspection and testing programme for its portable tools and leads. Explain how you would do it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first list every portable appliance and lead in a register, giving each one an ID number, its description, location and class. I would agree how often each type is checked, based on how hard it is used: site tools and leads more often than office equipment. I would train users to do a quick visual check before each use, looking for damaged cords, cracked plugs and burn marks, and to report problems. At each formal inspection and test, I would do a full visual inspection, then the earth continuity, insulation resistance and polarity tests as needed, and fix a dated pass label. Any item that fails would be labelled, taken out of use at once and either repaired or scrapped. All results, repairs and due dates go into the register, and I would review it to find items that fail often.
markingPoints: Register with ID, description, location and class
Inspection intervals based on use and risk
User checks before use and reporting
Formal inspection and tests with dated pass labels; failed items removed from use
Results, repairs and due dates recorded and reviewed

essays.stem: Explain why cords and extension leads overheat or fail in use, and how each cause can be prevented.
essays.modelAnswer: A cord that is too thin for the load carries more current than it is rated for, so it overheats; the cord must be rated above the appliance's current. A cable reel used while still coiled cannot lose heat, so it should be fully unwound when used near its rating. Plugging many appliances into one lead or adaptor adds their currents together and overloads it, so loads must be added up and spread. Loose terminals and worn socket contacts cause heat at the joint, so terminals must be tightened properly and worn sockets replaced. Cords crushed under doors, furniture or carpets, or pulled by the cord instead of the plug, are damaged inside, so cords must be routed safely and handled correctly. Sunlight, oil and water damage the wrong kind of sheath, so the right sheath must be chosen. Regular inspection finds these faults early.
markingPoints: Undersized cord: choose a cord rated above the load
Coiled reels: unwind fully
Overloading through multiple appliances or adaptors
Loose terminals, worn contacts, crushing and pulling by the cord
Wrong sheath for conditions; regular inspection

essays.stem: You supervise trainees fitting cords and plugs. Describe the common faults you would look for and how you would check their work.
essays.modelAnswer: Common faults are: the sheath not reaching into the cord grip, so the cores take the strain; a loose cord grip; cores stripped too far so bare conductor shows outside the terminal; nicked insulation or cut strands; loose strands outside the terminal; cores on the wrong terminals; the earth core not connected or cut shorter than the others; tinned ends in screw terminals; and covers not fitted properly. I would check each trainee's first plug with them, opening it to inspect every point, and then spot-check later work. I would ask them to explain why each step matters. Every finished item would be tested for earth continuity, insulation resistance and polarity before it is labelled. If I found a fault, I would have the trainee correct it and retest, and note it in their training record so we can practise that skill.
markingPoints: Names sheath and cord grip faults
Names stripping faults: bare conductor, nicks, loose strands, tinning
Names connection faults: wrong terminals, earth missing or short
Checks by opening and inspecting, then testing every item
Corrects, retests and records for training

essays.stem: Compare re-wireable plugs, moulded-on plugs and detachable cord sets. Explain how you would deal with damage to each.
essays.modelAnswer: A re-wireable plug can be opened, so its cord can be re-terminated or the plug replaced, but the quality depends on the person who wires it. If it is cracked or burnt, the plug is replaced and the cord end cut back to good cable. A moulded-on plug is sealed at the factory, so it is reliable and cannot be wired wrongly, but it cannot be opened. If it or the cord near it is damaged, the plug is cut off, destroyed at once so nobody can plug it in with live cut ends, and a suitable re-wireable plug is fitted, or the whole cord is replaced. A detachable cord set plugs into a socket on the appliance, so it is easy to change without opening the appliance. A damaged set is simply replaced with one of the same rating. In every case the item is tested and labelled after the repair.
markingPoints: Re-wireable: can be opened and repaired; quality depends on the wirer
Moulded: reliable and sealed; damaged plug cut off and destroyed, replaced
Detachable cord set: easy to swap; replace with the same rating
Explains why a cut-off moulded plug must be destroyed
Tests and labels after each repair

essays.stem: A customer brings in a fan whose cord has been joined with tape in two places. Explain how you would advise the customer, carry out the work and record it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would explain politely that taped joints are not safe: tape does not hold the cores together, the joint can pull apart or overheat, and bare copper can give a shock or start a fire. I would recommend replacing the whole cord, not making new joints, and give the customer a price for the cord, plug if needed, and labour, with GCT at the current rate, and get their agreement. With the fan unplugged, I would fit a new cord of the right type and rating, with the correct cord grips and terminations, and fit a suitable plug. I would test it for continuity, insulation resistance and polarity, and an earth continuity test if the fan has an earth. I would record the cord type, plug, test results and price on the job card, fix a pass label, and show the customer the old cord.
markingPoints: Explains the dangers of taped joints in plain words
Recommends replacing the whole cord; gives a price with GCT and gets agreement
Fits the right cord and plug correctly with the fan unplugged
Tests appropriate to the fan's class
Records the job, labels the fan and shows the old cord

practical1.title: Select, fit and test cords and plugs for three different items
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group three items, each with a damaged or missing cord: a metal-bodied (Class I) 110 V appliance, a double-insulated (Class II) appliance, and a 220 V portable machine. For each item, read the nameplate, work out the current, and choose the cord type, number of cores, size and plug from the Centre's stock, writing down the reason for each choice. Share the items so each member fits at least one cord or plug end while the assessor watches, and another member checks it before the cover goes on. Remove the old cords and make cut-off moulded plugs unusable. Fit the new cords at both ends with the correct grips and terminations. Test each item (earth continuity where there is an earth, flexing the cord; insulation resistance; polarity), fix a pass label, and enter the item in an appliance register. None of the items is plugged in during the task; the instructor runs each one on the protected test bench at the end. Photograph each stage and hand in the selection sheet, the test results and the register page.
materials: A Class I 110 V appliance, a Class II appliance and a 220 V portable machine, each with a damaged or missing cord
Stock of flexible cords (two-core and three-core, PVC and rubber, different sizes)
110 V and 220 V plugs of the right patterns
Wire strippers, sheath stripper, side cutters, screwdrivers
Low-resistance ohmmeter or multimeter, insulation resistance tester
Pass labels, appliance register and selection sheet
photos: The three items with their nameplates, and the selection sheet
The old cords removed and the cut-off plugs made unusable
Inside a fitted plug, showing grip, earth length and terminals
Inside an appliance terminal area, showing the cord grip and routing
The earth continuity test with the cord being flexed
The pass labels fitted and the register page
checklist: Worked out the current and chose a suitable cord and plug, with reasons
Stripped sheath and cores correctly, with no nicks or loose strands
Held the sheath in the cord grip and left the earth core longer
Connected each core to the right terminal, tight, with no bare conductor showing
Checked another member's work before the cover went on
Carried out the right tests for each class and recorded results correctly
Made cut-off plugs unusable and kept the bench tidy
safety: No item is plugged in during the task; only the instructor runs them on the protected test bench
Check any appliance with a motor for a charged capacitor before touching its terminals
Use strippers and cutters away from your body and wear safety glasses
Keep test leads clear of your hands during the insulation resistance test

practical2.title: Make up a site extension lead, and inspect a batch of portable equipment
practical2.brief: Part A: the group makes up a heavy-duty extension lead for site use from rubber-sheathed three-core cord, with a plug at the supply end and a weatherproof socket or connector box at the far end. Use the cord data the assessor gives to work out the voltage drop for the planned length and load, and decide whether the length is acceptable on 110 V. Test the finished lead (earth continuity end to end while flexing, insulation resistance, polarity at the socket), label it, and enter it in the register. Part B: the assessor sets out eight portable items with faults planted in some of them (for example a taped joint, a loose cord grip, a missing earth, a cracked plug, reversed polarity, a cord too thin for the load). As a team, inspect and test each item, decide pass or fail, label it, and record the findings and actions in the register. Then repair two failed items and retest them. Each member inspects at least two items and explains one decision to the assessor. No item is plugged in. Photograph each stage and hand in the voltage drop sum, the test results and the register.
materials: Heavy-duty rubber-sheathed three-core cord, plug, weatherproof socket or connector box
Cord data (resistance per metre) from the assessor
Eight portable items prepared by the assessor
Spare cords, plugs and cord grips for repairs
Low-resistance ohmmeter or multimeter, insulation resistance tester
Pass and fail labels, appliance register
photos: The voltage drop sum and the decision on length
Both ends of the finished extension lead, opened, before the covers go on
The eight items laid out with their labels
A failed item after repair, with its new pass label
checklist: Worked out the voltage drop correctly and made a sound decision on length
Fitted the plug at the supply end and the socket at the far end
Terminated both ends correctly with grips holding the sheath
Tested the lead fully and labelled it
Found the planted faults in the items they inspected
Made safe pass or fail decisions and explained one clearly
Repaired and retested a failed item, and kept the register accurate
safety: No lead or item is plugged in during the task
Treat every item as faulty until it has been inspected and tested
Keep failed items labelled and apart so they cannot be used by mistake
Wear safety glasses when cutting and stripping cords
